justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with only modest drift over time. For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to recent observed levels, assuming mean-reversion tendencies and limited overnight catalysts would keep price action contained. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with longer-run trend momentum without assuming any sharp directional break. The one-month estimate at 400 is essentially a round-number anchor that reflects my uncertainty about direction at that horizon — I'm not strongly confident in either an upward or downward move, so the point estimate gravitates toward what I perceive as a near-term equilibrium zone.

Confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, realized volatility in the underlying asset constrains how far prices can plausibly move, so a 30-point range captures most scenarios. At one week, macro data releases, central bank communications, and positioning shifts can all meaningfully alter direction, so I widened the interval to roughly 50 points on each side. At one month, the range expands to 50 points in each direction from the point estimate, acknowledging that over four-plus weeks, trend reversals, sentiment shifts, and structural changes in supply-demand dynamics could all materialize in ways that are fundamentally unpredictable from current information.

The key risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macro shocks — an unexpected central bank policy decision, a geopolitical escalation, or a significant data surprise — any of which could generate moves well beyond the one-day or one-week bounds. On the upside, a strong risk-on sentiment surge or short squeeze dynamic could push prices above 423 or even 450 within a week. On the downside, a broad risk-off episode, liquidity crunch, or negative earnings/economic surprise could break below 372 or even 350 at the monthly horizon. Tail risks, by definition, are underweighted in interval construction, and I would note that fat-tailed return distributions in financial markets mean true extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a normal distribution would imply.
